# What a model needs {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Six questions, six packages

MODFLOW does not have a "model file." It has a **package per question**.

| Question | Package |
|---|---|
| What shape is the domain, and in what units? | `DIS` |
| Which cells are active, and where do we start? | `BAS` |
| How permeable is it? | `LPF` |
| Who is pumping? | `WEL` |
| What comes in from above? | `RCH` |
| How do we solve, and what do we save? | `PCG`, `OC` |

::: {.fragment}
That table *is* the mental model. Every model you build for the rest of the
semester is these six answers, occasionally plus a seventh.
:::

## Your turn: size the grid

Our basin is discretized at 250 m cells, 40 rows by 60 columns, one layer.
Work out how big the domain actually is, in kilometres.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_grid
nlay, nrow, ncol = 1, 40, 60
delr = delc = 250.0     # cell size, metres
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_grid
width_km = ______
height_km = ______
print(f"{width_km} km east-west by {height_km} km north-south")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_grid"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`delr` is the width of a column, so the east-west extent is set by `ncol`.
Metres to kilometres is a factor of 1000.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_grid"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
width_km = ncol * delr / 1000
height_km = nrow * delc / 1000
```

15 km by 10 km, in 2400 cells. Worth doing this arithmetic *before* you run
anything — a grid that turns out to be 15 m across is a mistake you want to
catch now, not after a twenty-minute solve.
:::
:::

# Writing it down {background-color="#AB0520"}

## Discretization

```python
mf = flopy.modflow.Modflow("scbasin", model_ws=ws, exe_name=mf2005)

flopy.modflow.ModflowDis(
    mf, nlay=1, nrow=40, ncol=60,
    delr=250.0, delc=250.0,      # cell size
    top=420.0, botm=340.0,       # elevations, not thicknesses
    nper=1, steady=True,         # one steady-state stress period
)
```

::: {.fragment}
`top` and `botm` are **elevations**, not thicknesses. Getting this backwards
produces a model with negative thickness that fails in a way the error message
does not explain.
:::

## Boundaries and starting heads

```python
ibound = np.ones((1, 40, 60), dtype=int)
ibound[:, :, 0] = -1        # constant head upgradient
ibound[:, :, -1] = -1       # constant head downgradient

strt = np.full((1, 40, 60), 412.0)
strt[:, :, -1] = 402.0

flopy.modflow.ModflowBas(mf, ibound=ibound, strt=strt)
```

::: {.fragment}
`ibound`: `1` active, `0` inactive, **`-1` constant head**. In a steady-state
run `strt` is only a starting guess *except* in the `-1` cells, where it is the
boundary condition itself.
:::

## Stresses

```python
flopy.modflow.ModflowLpf(mf, hk=12.0, laytyp=1, ipakcb=53)
flopy.modflow.ModflowWel(
    mf, stress_period_data={0: [[0, 20, 30, -4000.0]]}, ipakcb=53
)
flopy.modflow.ModflowRch(mf, rech=1.4e-4, ipakcb=53)
```

::: {.fragment}
The well entry is `[layer, row, column, rate]`, zero-indexed, and **negative is
extraction**. A sign error here is the single most common way to end up
presenting a mound where you meant a cone.
:::

## Your turn: the pumping rate

A water provider reports the well pumps **730 acre-feet per year**. MODFLOW
wants m³/day, negative for extraction.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_rate
acre_feet_per_year = 730.0
M3_PER_ACRE_FOOT = 1233.48
DAYS_PER_YEAR = 365.0
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_rate
rate_m3_per_day = ______
print(f"WEL rate: {rate_m3_per_day:.1f} m3/d")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_rate"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

Convert the volume first, then divide by the number of days.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_rate"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

Don't forget the sign. MODFLOW reads a positive `WEL` rate as *injection*.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_rate"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
rate_m3_per_day = -acre_feet_per_year * M3_PER_ACRE_FOOT / DAYS_PER_YEAR
```

About `-2466.9` m³/d. Roughly 60% of the 4000 m³/d we are about to simulate —
so expect a correspondingly shallower cone.
:::
:::

# Hitting go {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Run it, then check that it ran

```python
mf.write_input()
success, buff = mf.run_model(silent=True, report=True)

assert success, "MODFLOW did not converge:\n" + "\n".join(buff[-20:])
```

::: {.fragment}
**FloPy does not raise when a model fails to converge.** It returns
`(success, buff)` and carries on. If you ignore `success`, you will happily plot
the last thing that landed in the `.hds` file and present it as a result.
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
Every model you run in this course, from here to Week 15, gets that `assert`.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**`report=True` is not optional.** With `silent=True` alone FloPy hands back an
empty `buff`, so the assertion fires with no diagnostic in it — the one moment
you needed one.
:::

## Your turn: is that drawdown a lot?

The aquifer is 80 m thick and the well cell sits at the head printed above.
Express the drawdown as a percentage of saturated thickness.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_dd
head_at_well = 407.25
head_undisturbed = 410.42
aquifer_bottom = 340.0
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_dd
drawdown = ______
percent_of_thickness = ______
print(f"{drawdown:.2f} m, {percent_of_thickness:.1f}% of saturated thickness")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_dd"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Saturated thickness is the undisturbed head minus the aquifer bottom, not the
80 m you were told — that is the *geologic* thickness.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_dd"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
drawdown = head_undisturbed - head_at_well
percent_of_thickness = 100 * drawdown / (head_undisturbed - aquifer_bottom)
```

3.17 m, about 4.5% — small enough that the confined approximation holds. Above
roughly 25% you should be asking whether `laytyp=1` is doing real work.
:::
:::
